msItem.title: The Small Book of Commandments
ספר מצוות קטן
Sefer Mitsṿot Ḳatan

author.persName: Isaac ben Joseph, of Corbeil, active 13th century

msItem.note: With the glosses by Perez ben Elijah of Corbeil; without the introductory letter by the author.
The beginning of the index is wanting. To the end of the index are appended further prohibitions, mainly those found in Leviticus 18, which do not have numbers attached.

Several short, miscellaneous liturgical and halakhic items on ff. 6r-7v (between the end of the the index and the beginning of the main text), and on f. 67r-v (between the sections corresponding to the Fourth and Fifth Days), including an exposition on the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy (פרוש של שלש עשרה מידות; f. 67r-v) which is also by Isaac ben Joseph of Corbeil.

msItem.title: Ḥayyei ʿOlam
חיי עולם

respStmt.persName: Jonah ben Abraham Gerondi, approximately 1200-1263 יונה בן אברהם גירונדי

msItem.note: The title of this work as given in most printed editions and some later manuscripts is Sefer ha-Yirʾah (The Book of Awe) ספר היראה, but the majority of manuscripts witnesses (including all of the earlier ones) are entitled Ḥayyei ʿOlam.

The attribution of this work to Jonah Gerondi (which is only supported by a few of the later manuscripts) has been questioned by scholars, with some arguing in favour of an anonymous Ashkenazic author from the circle of the Rhineland Pietists; see Benjamin Richler, '"Sefer ha-Yirʾah" attributed to R. Jona Gherondi' (in Hebrew), Alei Sefer 8 (1980), pp. 51-9.

msItem.title: Sefer ha-Ḥasidut
ספר החסידות
msItem.note: This is a reworking of the Sefer Ḥasidim, which was circulated alongside the latter in some medieval manuscripts and early printed editions (including the 1528 Bologna edition where it appears as the first 152 sections of the larger work), and which has since been shown by scholars to be distinct from the Sefer Ḥasidim proper in its language, style and ethical teachings, all of which point to a place of composition not in the Rhineland but in northern France. See discussions on this text by Haym Soloveitchik (Collected Essays, Volume III, pp. 79-90), and Ivan G. Marcus (Sefer Hasidim and the Ashkenazic Book in Medieval Europe, pp. 36-41).
Other manuscripts where this text has been transmitted indepently of the Sefer Ḥasidim are Milan, Biblioteca Ambrosiana, MS X.111 sup., and Moscow, Russian State Library, MS Günzburg 103.32.
The text in this manuscript contains three times as many French glosses as the printed edition.

msItem.title: Prayers
תפלות
Tefilot
msItem.note: This textual unit (which includes prayers for mourning, marriages and circumscision as well as for constructing an eruv, for reading the megillah and for the amelioration of dreams, is now incomplete; it appears that a later user had excised two folios from between ff. 52 and 53 (the stubs of these folios can be seen near the gutter).

msItem.title: Piyyutim for the Bridegroom
פיוטים לחתן
Piyyutim le-Ḥatan
msItem.note: Liturgical poems in honour of the bridegroom, some of which are by Simeon bar Isaac and identified as such by a later hand.

msItem.title: Order of the reading of the Torah
סדר קריאת התורה במועדים
Siddur ḳeriʾat ha-Torah be-moʿadim
msItem.note: Includes lists of Torah and haftarah readings for festivals, and of haftarah readings for regular Sabbaths throughout the year.

msItem.title: Templates for legal documents
טופסי שטרות
Ṭofsei shetarot
msItem.note: One of the templates (for a betrothal document; f. 157v) has been attributed by the scribe to Rabbis Shneʾor שניאור and Itzḥaḳ 'Shira Benish (Sire Benois?)'יצחק המכונה שירא בנייש of Alluy or Alloue (?) ('דאלוייאה'); see Gross, Gallia Judaica, pp. 58-9. It is also possible that the place name is a corrupted version of Évreux, in which case the rabbis cited would most likely be the well-known Isaac of Évreux and his father Shneur.

On f. 161, the two templates for excommunication (ḥerem) documents have been copied in a different hand, which is roughly contemporary to that of the scribe. The opening words of the second document have been copied out for a second time just beneath it, by a later hand (probably from the fifteenth century).

supportDesc.condition: Ff. 1-8 have sustained some minor damage, which has resulted in some loss of text; the damaged areas have been repaired using patches of paper. The lower half of f. 129 has been cut off.

handNote.p: According to the scribal colophon on f. 151r (at the end of No. 3), the scribe Mosheh b. Yitsḥak משה בן יצחק finished copying Nos. 1-3 on 8 Tammuz 5059 (9 June 1299); he copied the works for his own use. The name Mosheh משה has been picked out by means of dotted lines throughout the manuscript.

There are several lacunae in the manuscript: between ff. 56 and 58, between ff. 59 and 61, and between ff. 67 and 75. Presumably, these folios were lost within a century after the production of the manuscript, since replacement folios containing some of the missing text were supplied by a late-fourteenth-century Ashkenazic hand. The replacement folios ff. 57 and 60, however, are problematic in several ways: they are now separated by two folios, even though the text on f. 60r follows directly from f. 57v; f. 57r repeats a significant portion of the text already found on f. 59r-v); finally, even though f. 57 is now placed between ff. 56 and 58, the lacuna in the text between these two folios has not been filled.

history.acquisition: It belonged to the library of David Oppenheim (1664-1736), which was purchased by the Bodleian Library in 1829.
